notes: Inventory built from four independent general dictionaries, one pronunciation reference, one etymology reference and two domain references before the article was compared against it.

source_first_audit.profile_reason: integrate carries eight article senses across general combining, social membership, the American racial sense, the participial adjective and calculus, so the bounded inventory needs the extended source and fact allowance.

coverage_axes.notes: Four independent general dictionaries cover the combining, social, American racial and calculus senses and the adjective.
Transitive, intransitive, reflexive, passive, attributive and calculus frames each have an independent source.
integration, integrated, integrator, integrative, integrity and differentiate are each attested separately.
The American racial-integration use and the calculus use are checked against a dictionary and a domain reference each.
Adverb collocations, the American label and the different Northern Irish reading of integrated school are sourced.
One pronunciation reference and one etymology reference cover both transcriptions and the Latin origin.

facts.statement: integrate combines two or more things so that they work as one more effective whole
facts.source_detail: Cambridge gives the transitive combining sense with the sales and marketing department example.

facts.statement: integrate helps a person become part of a group, and is also used of the person becoming part of that group
facts.source_detail: Cambridge lists both the causative use for helping someone join a group and the plain use for becoming part of one.

facts.statement: integrate is used both with a direct object and without one, and takes into and with
facts.source_detail: Cambridge marks transitive and intransitive uses and shows integrate into and integrate with.

facts.statement: integrate ends the separation of people by race, sex or national origin in an organization or in society
facts.source_detail: Cambridge gives the desegregation sense with the armed forces example.

facts.statement: integrate oneself takes a reflexive object in integrate oneself into a group
facts.source_detail: Cambridge's induction-programme example shows new staff members integrating themselves into the team.

facts.statement: integrate occurs without an object in integrate with one's colleagues and integrate socially
facts.source_detail: Cambridge shows Dave finding it hard to integrate with his colleagues and work that seems to have integrated socially.

facts.statement: integrate forms, coordinates or blends separate things into a functioning or unified whole
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's first transitive sense is to form, coordinate, or blend into a functioning or unified whole; unite.

facts.statement: integrate incorporates something into a larger unit, or unites it with something else
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's second transitive sense is to incorporate into a larger unit and to unite with something else.

facts.statement: integrate desegregates an institution and brings people into equal membership in society or an organization
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's third transitive sense is to desegregate and to end the segregation of and bring into equal membership.

facts.statement: integrate finds the integral of a function or equation
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's fourth transitive sense is to find the integral of something such as a function or equation.

facts.statement: integrate has an intransitive use glossed as to become integrated
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster lists an intransitive entry for integrate meaning to become integrated.

facts.statement: integrative is an adjective meaning serving to integrate or directed toward integration
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster defines integrative as serving to integrate or favoring integration.

facts.statement: integrator is a noun for one that integrates, especially a device that adds variable quantities like mathematical integration
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster defines integrator as one that integrates, especially a device or computer unit comparable to mathematical integration.

sources.title: Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English: integrate, integrated

facts.statement: integrate takes into for the receiving whole, as in integrating new ideas into the traditional course structure
facts.source_detail: Longman's integrate into example is the department successfully integrating new ideas into the traditional course structure.

facts.statement: integrate takes with for the matching counterpart, as in integrating one rail network with another
facts.source_detail: Longman's integrate with examples are the Italian railway network with other European networks and a computer program with existing programs.

facts.statement: integrate is commonly modified by completely, fully, seamlessly, thoroughly, properly and successfully
facts.source_detail: Longman's corpus notes list these adverbs as the usual modifiers of integrate.

facts.statement: integrated appears in the passive with in, as in disabled students are integrated in regular classrooms
facts.source_detail: Longman's corpus examples include disabled students being integrated in regular classrooms and services being fully integrated.

facts.statement: integrated is an adjective for a system or institution that combines many different groups, ideas or parts so that they work well
facts.source_detail: Longman defines the adjective integrated with the integrated transport system example.

facts.statement: integrate is used of people becoming fully integrated into a local community
facts.source_detail: Longman's example is that they soon became fully integrated into the local community.

facts.statement: integrated describes something in which many different parts are closely connected and work successfully together
facts.source_detail: Oxford's first adjective sense is in which many different parts are closely connected and work successfully together.

facts.statement: integrated describes a school or institution that includes people from different races, sexes or religions who were previously separated
facts.source_detail: Oxford's second adjective sense covers integrated institutions intended for use by all races or religious groups.

facts.statement: vertically integrated describes unified control of all stages of production from raw materials to distribution
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster and Collins gloss vertically integrated as unified control of all aspects of industrial production through distribution.

facts.statement: integrate is given for Standard Southern British as /ˈɪn.tɪ.ɡɹeɪt/ with an /ˈɪn.tə.ɡɹeɪt/ variant
facts.source_detail: Wiktionary lists the British pronunciation with the second-syllable vowel written /ɪ/ and a /ə/ variant.

facts.statement: integrate is given for General American as /ˈɪn.təˌɡɹeɪt/ with secondary stress on the third syllable
facts.source_detail: Wiktionary lists the General American pronunciation with a secondary stress mark before the third syllable.

facts.statement: integrate carries primary stress on the first syllable in both British and American transcriptions
facts.source_detail: Both Wiktionary transcriptions place the primary stress mark before the first syllable.

facts.statement: integrate is attested as an adjective from the 1450s before the verb, and the adjective is not the modern general form
facts.source_detail: Wiktionary records the adjective from the 1450s and the verb from the seventeenth century as separate parts of speech.

facts.statement: integrate comes from Latin integratus, past participle of integrare to make whole, from integer whole
facts.source_detail: Etymonline derives integrate from Latin integratus, the past participle of integrare, from integer.

facts.statement: integer is literally untouched, from in- not plus the root of tangere to touch
facts.source_detail: Etymonline glosses Latin integer as whole, complete, literally untouched, from in- not and the root of tangere.

facts.statement: integrate is recorded as a verb from the 1630s meaning to render something whole by bringing together its parts
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates the verb to the 1630s with the sense to render (something) whole, bring together the parts of.

facts.statement: integration is recorded from the 1610s as the act of bringing together the parts of a whole
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates integration to the 1610s from Late Latin integrationem.

facts.statement: integrity is from about 1400, from Latin integritatem soundness, wholeness, completeness
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates integrity to around 1400 from Old French integrite and Latin integritatem.

sources.title: Wikipedia: School integration in the United States; Integrated education in Northern Ireland

facts.statement: integrate names the American process of ending race-based segregation in public and private schools
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia describes school integration in the United States as the process of ending race-based segregation in American schools.

facts.statement: integrated names schools in Northern Ireland that teach Catholic and Protestant children together rather than schools defined by race
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia describes Northern Irish integrated schools as bringing together children from Catholic, Protestant and other backgrounds.

facts.statement: integrate is contrasted in American civil-rights writing with desegregation, which removes the legal separation without producing a mixed body
facts.source_detail: Reporting on American schools distinguishes legally desegregated schools that remain almost entirely single-race from integrated ones.

facts.statement: integrate is performed with respect to a named variable, written as an integral of f(x) with dx
facts.source_detail: The Integral article writes definite and indefinite integrals with respect to a variable of integration marked by dx.

facts.statement: integrate is performed over an interval from a lower limit to an upper limit for a definite integral
facts.source_detail: The Integral article defines the definite integral over an interval bounded by limits a and b.

facts.statement: integrate is done by parts as a named standard technique, and numerically when no closed form exists
facts.source_detail: The Integral article lists integration by parts among the standard techniques and numerical integration for cases without a closed form.

facts.statement: differentiate is the inverse operation of integration under the fundamental theorem of calculus
facts.source_detail: The Integral article states that integration is the inverse operation of differentiation.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate combines separate elements, functions or units so that the whole works as one
source_union.rationale: Three independent general dictionaries give the transitive combining sense and both prepositional frames, so the article's sense 1 stays inside the bounded source set.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrated is an established adjective for a whole whose many parts are closely connected and work together
source_union.rationale: Two independent learner dictionaries list the adjective separately from the verb, which supports a numbered participial-adjective sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate is used without an object of systems and services that come to work together
source_union.rationale: The intransitive entry and the integrate-with frame support a separate intransitive sense for things rather than people.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate takes a person or group as object when an institution makes them a full member of a community
source_union.rationale: The causative use with a personal object and the reflexive frame are attested independently of the combining sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate is used without an object of a person who becomes a full member of a group or community
source_union.rationale: The objectless personal use, the passive with in, and the fully integrated into a community example support a separate intransitive sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate ends racial separation in an American institution and brings people into equal membership
source_union.rationale: Two general dictionaries plus the domain reference support the American racial sense and its contrast with desegregate.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrated describes an American school, district or neighbourhood that is no longer racially separated
source_union.rationale: The learner dictionary adjective sense and the domain reference support the labelled adjective sense and the different Northern Irish reading.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate finds the integral of a function with respect to a variable, over limits, by parts or numerically
source_union.rationale: The dictionary sense fixes the lexical meaning and the domain reference fixes the frames and the inverse relation to differentiation.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate carries first-syllable primary stress, with a British and American difference in the second-syllable vowel and the third-syllable secondary stress
source_union.rationale: The pronunciation reference fixes both transcriptions and the separate adjective form, so the article states only differences the symbols show.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate descends from Latin integer whole and keeps a modern core of making separate things into one undivided whole
source_union.rationale: The etymology reference supports the origin, the dating hedge and the related words, and the shared core that the core-image branches use.

source_union.canonical_statement: the integrate family produces integration, integrated, integrating, integrator, integrative and disintegrate
source_union.rationale: The derived forms listed in the article each have an independent dictionary or etymology entry in the bounded source set.
